item.title: How Sweden went from asylum haven to enacting Europe’s strictest migration policies
item.description: The political consensus that emerged in little under a decade is for the country to maintain restrictive migration policies.
item.content:encoded:
For decades, Sweden was known as one of Europe’s most welcoming countries for refugees. It took pride in pursuing one of Europe’s most generous asylum policies, and often presented itself as a humanitarian role model.

But today it has one of the continent’s most restrictive migration policies. That transformation has taken little more than a decade.

The turning point came during the 2015 refugee crisis. Sweden received more than 160,000 asylum applications, more than 12% of all applications in the European Union. Around 35,000 were unaccompanied minors, more than one third of the EU total that year. The scale of the inflow exposed strains on the country’s system and fundamentally changed the political debate around migration.

The immediate response was a broad cross-party agreement introducing stricter asylum and family migration rules. This was followed by temporary border controls, and the replacement of permanent residence permits with temporary ones for most refugees.

These measures, introduced by a leftwing Social Democratic government, were more than a response to an exceptional situation. They signalled the emergence of a new political consensus: that Sweden should pursue a substantially more restrictive migration policy.

item.title: Karnataka to sing only two stanzas of ‘Vande Mataram’ at state events
item.description: All six stanzas will be sung during functions attended by the president, vice president, prime minister or governor, the state government said.
item.content:encoded:
The Congress government in Karnataka has ordered that only the first two stanzas of Vande Mataram be sung at official programmes and functions, except those attended by the president, vice president, prime minister or governor, PTI reported.

On January 28, the Union home ministry directed that all six stanzas of the Vande Mataram be sung first when it is played together with the national anthem Jana Gana Mana.

Only the first two stanzas of the national song had been played at official functions earlier. The remaining stanzas, which invoke Hindu goddesses Durga, Lakshmi and Saraswati, had been omitted.

The Bharatiya Janata Party has long alleged that the Congress had agreed to drop the four stanzas to “appease Muslims”.

On August 19, The Congress said that the party would sing only the first two stanzas of Vande Mataram at its functions, citing a Congress Working Committee resolution from 1937.

In December, Prime Minister Narendra Modi criticised the Congress in Parliament, alleging that Jawaharlal Nehru, India’s first prime minister, had supported Muhammad Ali Jinnah in opposing Vande Mataram when the resolution was adopted because it could “irritate Muslims”.

In August, the Prevention of Insults to National Honour Amendment Act, which criminalises insults to the national song, came into effect.

item.title: Natalie Portman biofic? The controversy over Rachel Cusk’s ‘Life of M’ misses the point
item.description: Close to publication, speculation about its subject matter began to brew, with reports that the title character was based on film star Natalie Portman.
item.content:encoded:
Rachel Cusk is prone to controversy. Her clinical gaze and razor-sharp brilliance, across a range of novels and memoirs, have long divided critical opinion, earning her a formidable reputation for both literary genius and personal cruelty. Her latest book, Life of M, is no exception.

The novel is premised on a writer’s casual offer to compose the autobiography of M, an actor, who, being a “good sport”, agrees. The pair live on opposite sides of the same city and share a couple of mutual friends. But while the writer suffers from low self-worth, they (a gender-neutral presence) see the rich and famous M’s “distance from the random violence of insignificance” as equally problematic.

Identities are collapsed from the outset by the writer’s proposal to work on M’s “autobiography”, rather than her biography, and not as a ghostwriter. Initially, this doesn’t appear to make sense, but given the way the novel plays with the indeterminacy of the self, it’s a very deliberate statement.

As you might expect of Cusk, what follows is an interrogation of ideas about selfhood and character, rather than a traditional story, as she considers authenticity and pretence through the lens of M, the consummate performer. The tangle of autofiction is further reinforced by a series...

item.title: Flu shots prevent serious illness but why don’t many Indians take them?
item.description: Amid a surge in flu cases, doctors say annual vaccination will help many Indians, yet national immunisation programmes don’t include the shot.
item.content:encoded:
Aarti Rawal* is a 27-year-old resident of Delhi. In 2025 for the first time, Rawal took the flu vaccine on her doctor’s recommendation, “after a spell of long Covid in 2023 and 2024 messed up my health”, she said. “I’d get recurrent bronchial attacks exacerbated by winter pollution.”

When she repeated the shot in spring this year, she got her family to take it as well, even though they showed some reluctance. “They didn’t think it was necessary,” said Rawal.

Despite frequent travel within India and abroad, Rawal noticed that she was not falling sick as much as before, which, she said, “was a welcome relief”.

She has also been spared, so far, during Delhi’s present surge in influenza cases.

ISignal spoke with four doctors, all of whom affirmed Rawal’s experience in the context of the present surge of swine flu: People of all ages, including children, who have taken the flu shot have either not fallen sick, or experience milder symptoms.

Swine flu, also known as H1N1 flu based on the virus that causes it, is categorised as Influenza A, a serious form of the flu in terms of morbidity and mortality. India typically sees two influenza seasons, one from January to March and the other after the monsoon sets in.

item.title: From a Kashmir anthology: From childhood to death, a man watches his mother struggle with loneliness
item.description: An excerpt from Hriday Kaul Bharati’s short story in ‘The Big Book of Kashmiri Literature: Poems, Songs, Plays, Stories,’ edited by Onaiza Drabu.
item.content:encoded:
As she worked the mud plaster onto the wall, she reached the doorpost and paused to rest for a moment. She might have wanted to daub the wall above it as well, but it rose far above her … so high that even with her arms stretched up, it was impossible to reach. She glanced around the empty room, her eyes drifting from one wall to the next. Grabbing the smearing mop, she searched for a way to reach the wall over the doorpost.

Her gaze stopped at me and, for a while, she forgot her work. I had reached that stage of life when a human, newly past crawling, begins practising standing on two feet. My attempts had left a few circles of stains on the floor during her mopping.

“My scruffy one,” she said, “please don’t leave behind these circles!”

But there was no real complaint in her voice. Instead, she was pleased that I’d crossed an important milestone of the crawling era and was now gathering myself to stand on two feet. item.title: Xi Jinping to attend BRICS summit in New Delhi, China confirms
item.description: This will be the Chinese president’s first visit to India in nearly seven years and since the 2020 military standoff.
item.content:encoded:
Chinese President Xi Jinping will visit India for the first time in nearly seven years to attend the 18th BRICS Summit in New Delhi on September 12 and September 13, China’s foreign ministry said on Thursday.

The visit comes as India-China relations have seen a thaw since 2024, following years of tensions over a military standoff in Ladakh.

Meanwhile, Bangladesh said that it will not send a government representative to the summit.

Xi last visited India in October 2019, when he met Prime Minister Narendra Modi in Tamil Nadu’s Mamallapuram. The two leaders are now expected to meet on the sidelines of the BRICS summit.

The BRICS grouping comprises India, Brazil, Russia, China, Saudi Arabia, South Africa, Egypt, Ethiopia, Indonesia, Iran and the United Arab Emirates.

Border tensions between India and China escalated in June 2020 when a violent face-off between Indian and Chinese soldiers took place in Ladakh’s Galwan Valley along the Line of Actual Control. It led to the deaths of 20 Indian soldiers. Beijing said that the clash left four of its soldiers dead.

Following the military face-off, both countries deployed thousands of soldiers along with heavy artillery in the region. China and India held several rounds of military and diplomatic talks to resolve their border standoff.

Adhikari said that Shastri was only sharing his views and not imposing them on anyone.

On Sunday, Shastri, the head of the Bageshwar Dham temple, said that he does not like it when “dirty” non-vegetarian food is eaten during the Hindu festival and at gatherings linked to the celebration. Meat must not be sold near the goddess’ idol during the festival, he added. The festival will begin on October 6 and conclude on October 10 this year.

Among Bengali Hindus, eating meat during Durga Puja is common and animal sacrifice is also an important ritual for some in the community.

Shastri had called for these restriction at a religious event at Liluah in Howrah. Adhikari, along with his Cabinet colleagues from the Bharatiya Janata Party, had met him and hosted a dinner for him on Friday.

The comments by Shastri had triggered a row in the state. Protests were held by Congress workers, with some persons reportedly burning photographs of Shastri outside the Bhawanipore police station in Kolkata, The Hindu reported.

item.title: SC rejects gangster Abu Salem’s plea for early release in 1993 Mumbai blasts case
item.description: The gangster had argued that the remission he earned for good conduct and undertrial custody should be counted toward computing his 25-year jail term.
item.content:encoded:
The Supreme Court on Thursday dismissed a petition filed by gangster Abu Salem seeking early release from prison in the 1993 Mumbai serial bomb blasts case, Bar and Bench reported.

Salem had contended that the remission he had earned for good conduct and undertrial custody should be counted toward the computation of his 25-year jail sentence, after completion of which he would be eligible for early release.

Remission is the reduction of the duration of a prison sentence without changing its nature, allowing for earlier release.

In September 2017, a special court under the Terrorist and Disruptive Activities Prevention Act in Mumbai sentenced Salem to life imprisonment for his role in the blasts that killed more than 250 persons.

He had been extradited from Portugal in November 2005.

Salem’s petition centred around the terms of the extradition treaty between India and Portugal under which he would have to be released on completion of 25 years in jail.

He had argued that the remission for good conduct and the undertrial custody amounts to more than three years, which needed to be set off against his full sentence. Based on this, Salem contended that he had completed his 25-year term by March 31, 2025.

The Maharashtra government maintained that Salem had not completed 25 years.

item.title: War history: How India fought against Pakistan’s military attack in the Rann of Kutch in 1965
item.description: An excerpt from ‘The Sabre Slayers: The Air Battles of the 1965 War with Pakistan’, by Philip Rajkumar and Shiv Kunal Verma.
item.content:encoded:
Since Partition in August 1947, Pakistan had laid claim to the northern half of the Great Rann of Kutch, up to the line of 24 degrees north latitude, covering an area of more than 9,000 square kilometres, on the following grounds.

The first argument was that the Rann of Kutch could either be considered a landlocked sea or a boundary lake, and therefore the international boundary should run through the middle.

The second argument was that the northern half of the Rann had been administered by Sindh since its annexation by the British in 1843. Several pre- and post-Partition documents were cited in support of this claim.

In the third week of January 1965, a patrol of Gujarat Police discovered a newly built 30-kilometre-long track running from Surai to the east inside Pakistan to Kanjarkot in the west inside Indian territory. For most of its length, the track ran more than 2 kilometres inside Indian territory. The fort at Kanjarkot was briefly occupied by Pakistani Rangers, but they vacated it after a short stay. India launched a diplomatic protest about this incursion, which was followed by a counter-protest by the other side.

item.title: ‘Singh doesn’t know how to drive’: US Homeland Security gets flak for ‘anti-Indian’ post
item.description: The social media post had an AI-generated image featuring Transformers character Optimus Prime and a brown man staring at each other.
item.content:encoded:
A social media post by the United States’ Department of Homeland Security that said “Mr Singh does not know how to drive” drew flak online, with politicians and Indian diaspora groups criticising it for being racist.

The post on social media platform X on Wednesday had an artificial intelligence-generated poster featuring Transformers character Optimus Prime and a brown man staring at each other. “Self-deport or find out”, read the image.

“America for Americans,” the poster said. “Get off our roads, you don't know how to drive Mr Singh.”

The appearance of the man in the image was similar to that of an Indian-origin truck driver arrested in Florida in August 2025 for a crash that killed three persons.

The post had been viewed more than 4.2 million times as of 12 noon Indian time on Thursday, with more than a thousand reposts. It was posted as a reply to a video by the department itself urging people to report allegedly undocumented migrants living in the US.

item.title: How Ahmedabad became an unwelcoming city
item.description: The city has a history of political organising and public debate. So why was a group who had gathered to read books in a park attacked by Hindutva supporters?
item.content:encoded:
In 1972, community organiser Ela Bhatt and a group of women met at Ahmedabad’s Victoria Garden to discuss the conditions in which self-employed women worked. That meeting led to the formation of the Self-Employed Women’s Association, or SEWA, which became one of India’s most significant labour organisations.

Ahmedabad’s public spaces have never just been places to pass the time: since the freedom struggle, they have hosted many important gatherings meant to organise, debate and build political movements.

That history makes the attack on a reading gathering at AUDA Garden in Vastrapur on August 27 particularly revealing. A group of people had gathered to read books including Anne Frank’s diary, Malala Yousafzai’s I Am Malala, Bhagat Singh’s Why I Am an Atheist and George Orwell’s 1984. Members of the Bajrang Dal disrupted the gathering and assaulted some of those present.

The organisation later said its objection was directed at Yousafzai, citing her views on Pakistan and Kashmir. The incident followed a controversy at a school in the city, where members of the Bajrang Dal and Akhil Bharatiya Vidyarthi Parishad – Hindutva groups under the umbrella of the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh – objected to the inclusion of I Am Malala and Anne Frank’s diary in the school’s reading programme.

item.title: An activist writes how the Chipko Movement inspired him to conserve forests in South India

item.title: Behind deaths of Adivasi children in Balaghat: appalling vaccination levels, widespread hunger
item.description: The outbreak became deadlier for the children because many of them were malnourished.
item.content:encoded:
In June, one-year-old Sahil caught a fever and developed a rash all over his body. A month later, he was dead, mostly likely from a measles-malaria outbreak that ripped through Madhya Pradesh’s Balaghat district.

Sahil’s 12-year-old sister Lamnin fell ill with similar symptoms and died a day later at their home in Bondari village.

As Scroll reported in the first part of this series, at least 25 children from the Baiga and Gond tribes have died since May in this remote Adivasi habitation in Madhya Pradesh. For two months, the outbreak went undetected because of the complete absence of a healthcare system in the area.

Measles is a disease that can be prevented through vaccination. India added the measles vaccine to its universal immunisation programme in 1985.

But four decades later, in the villages of Balaghat, we found that immunisation drives against measles existed only on paper.

“Why should I lie?”

Sahil’s father Samaroo Dhurwey said that neither Sahil nor Lamlin had been vaccinated against measles.

Dhurwey told Scroll that none of his seven children had ever been immunised against any disease. His eldest daughter is married, and the youngest is five years old.

item.title: William T Vollmann has written a 3,000‑page novel when the world appears to be done with big books

item.content:encoded:
With forecasters of doom debating the end of reading, of publishing and of literacy in general, what should we make of William T Vollmann’s forthcoming novel, A Table for Fortune?

Spanning four volumes at 3,000 pages, is it madness? A determined attempt to silence print’s naysayers?

I have been writing about Vollmann’s works since I penned the introduction to “William T Vollmann: A Critical Companion” more than 10 years ago.

The 67-year-old author has spent his career going big, in every sense, and I would not be the first to describe his approach to his art as uncompromising.

His projects grapple with weighty matters such as global poverty, the history of North America and climate change. Few of his roughly 25 books run under 500 pages. About half try to keep his readers engaged for several hundred pages beyond that. Many of them supplement the text with photographs, epigraphs, glossaries, family trees, sketches, timelines, variant tables of contents, alternating fonts and notes to the reader. The essay “Rising Up and Rising Down,” his philosophical and journalistic inquiry into the nature of violence, clocks in at over 3,000 pages across seven volumes.

item.title: Nepal floods halt contentious hydropower exports to Bangladesh via India

item.content:encoded:
Monsoon rains have routinely given Nepal a surge of hydropower, creating a surplus. Some of that surplus was used to supplement downstream neighbour Bangladesh’s fossil-fuel-dependent electricity supply.

On August 2, however, Nepal’s hydropower system was damaged extensively. Flash floods swept through the Bhotekoshi and Trishuli river systems, killing at least 1,250 people as of 3 September. The floods also damaged 15 hydropower plants and critical transmission infrastructure, wiping out over 750 MW of electricity generation, reported Time. Nearly 900 hydropower workers are missing.

The disaster has now disrupted Nepal’s electricity exports, with supplies to Bangladesh halted, authorities in Dhaka and Kathmandu confirmed to Dialogue Earth.

On September 3, Shaligram Bhandari, a spokesperson for Nepal’s Ministry of Energy, Water Resources and Irrigation, told Dialogue Earth that floods damaged the 22 megawatt Chilime and 24 MW Trishuli hydropower projects, which have since stopped generating electricity. The power they produced had been approved for export to Bangladesh. Nepal halted all power exports, Reuters reported several days earlier.

Amid the disaster, the ministry had yet to explore alternatives, Bhandari said. Nepal’s growing role as a hydropower exporter must be viewed together with these vulnerabilities.

The economy is not creating enough good jobs for young people, even if more were to pursue higher education and the examination system functioned smoothly. More technology to fix the examination system will not solve the deeper problem of the economy.

Moreover, there is increasing evidence that use of more technology and AI will worsen India’s unemployment crisis. While it may be unclear whether AI will create more jobs ultimately, it is sufficiently clear that inequality will rise during the transition, increasing further the distance between “haves” and “have nots”.

item.title: Can you teach yourself to detect AI writing? Maybe
item.description: A new study has found that the spread of LLMs is associated with lower variation in writing style.
item.content:encoded:
AI is quietly reshaping writing. It’s not just that prose is changing – the very structure of written language is genuinely changing too.

It’s not just a new technology.

It’s not a fad.

It’s an undeniable revolution.

Did this article’s introduction seem AI-generated? What made you feel that way?

The truth is, it was not AI-generated; I wrote it to emulate synthetic prose, the kind you get when a large language model (LLM) organises words into text.

That kind of prose suddenly seems to be everywhere: on low-quality websites built to accumulate advertising clicks, in social media captions chasing engagement, and even book manuscripts. Crime novelist Jerry Falade recently lost a book deal worth more than $2 million after his literary agents said they could no longer faithfully determine how his manuscript had come together. Hachette pulled the horror novel Shy Girl in March this year under similar suspicion.

Before generative AI, we could generally assume that written text had been composed by a human. This is no longer the case. So how can we spot AI-written text?

Pointing to the farm pond, or khet talab, dug on his land, Yadav said the difference from last year was stark. “Look at this, how little water is in my pond this time. Last year around this time, the entire pond was full. I used that water in October-November to irrigate my wheat crop. In Japan, there is a saying that you are never more than five minutes away from a curry shop. (For authentic Indian food, you have to go to an indoryori restaurant.)

From 2001 to 2007, there was even a curry museum in Yokohama, a sort of curry theme park featuring hostesses wearing saris, exhibits on the history of curry and spices, and a food court that served an array of curries and dishes made with curry powder, including Okinawan curry made with sake, an omelette-rice curry, a curry cocktail and curry chocolate.

A Japanese curry is a distinctive dish. It consists of chunks of meat (usually chicken, beef and shrimp), carrots, onions and potatoes simmered in an ochre-coloured, currypowder-flavoured, slightly sweetish sauce. The sweetness comes from apples or honey. Often a fried pork cutlet (tonkatsu) is placed on top. item.title: CJI asks Aravallis panel if it is waiting for him to retire; SC declines six-month extension

The Supreme Court on Monday refused to give a six-month extension to a committee it had constituted to submit a report on defining the Aravallis, The Indian Express reported.

Chief Justice Surya Kant questioned the panel’s request for time till February 28 to submit its conclusions, asking whether it was waiting for his retirement.

However, the bench comprising Kant and Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana allowed the committee to submit its report by November 30, two months after the August 31 deadline.

item.title: Why do people respond differently to mosquito bites? A scientist explains
item.description: The reaction reflects a complex interaction between mosquito saliva and the immune system.
item.content:encoded:
Two people spend an evening in the same garden and receive roughly the same number of mosquito bites. By morning, one barely notices them – while the other is covered in large, swollen, intensely itchy welts that linger for days.

Most of us have experienced this, or know someone who has. But why is it that mosquito bites affect some people so differently? The answer lies in the way a mosquito’s saliva interacts with our unique immune system.

When a mosquito bites you, they inject saliva into your skin. The immune system recognises the saliva as foreign and releases histamine – an immune cell chemical that causes allergy symptoms such as redness, swelling and itchiness.

But this only partly explains what’s going on. A mosquito’s saliva also contains a range of other biologically active compounds that interact with the immune system in more complex ways than once assumed.

For instance, a mosquito’s saliva also contains proteins that prevent blood clotting and keep blood flowing so they can feed undisturbed.

These same salivary proteins influence the immune response that occurs at the bite site. Rather than acting solely as a feeding aid, mosquito saliva can alter the local immune environment within minutes of a bite.

When Osama Manzar started the nonprofit Digital Empowerment Foundation in 2002, just 1.2% of India’s population was online. Now, more than 70% is. But Manzar’s mission statement – helping poor and rural communities come out of the digital dark to access information, literacy, and livelihoods – still holds.

In the age of artificial intelligence, Manzar senses the risk of another extractive technology, with the benefits and control concentrated among powerful actors both at the algorithmic level and in terms of land and water.

item.title: Maharashtra: VHP calls for barring Muslims from garba events, demands Aadhaar checks
item.description: The Vishva Hindu Parishad said that organisers must apply a tilak on the foreheads of those participating in the Hindu festival.
item.content:encoded:
The Vishva Hindu Parishad has called for a ban on Muslims from taking part in garba events in Maharashtra and set “guidelines” for the organisers to verify the identity of participants, India Today reported on Sunday.

The measures include checking the Aadhaar cards of those participating and applying a tilak, a sacred mark on the forehead in Hindu tradition, on the participants.

VHP spokesperson Shriraj Nair said that the Hindutva group had decided to prevent Muslims from participating in garba events, arguing that the festival is centred on worshipping a Hindu deity, India Today reported.

Garba is a Gujarati folk dance, performed in a circular pattern around a lamp or idol, symbolising the Hindu deity Durga. It is performed during the festival of Navratri, which will begin on October 11 and end on October 20 this year.

“Navratri is not just about songs and dance,” Nair was quoted as saying. “The festival is about worshipping the goddess. Why should Muslims, who are against idol worship, participate in the festival?”

When Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh chief Mohan Bhagwat arrived in Britain on September 3 on the last leg of an international tour that had started in the US on August 25 and also taken him to Canada, no exact schedule had been made public.

Despite not having any confirmation of his movements, protesters gathered outside Parliament Square in London on Sunday, the day before Bhagwat’s visit was expected to conclude.

With the Houses of Parliament and Big Ben serving as a symbolic backdrop, the demonstrators aimed to send two messages: that they rejected the Hindu majoritarianism of the RSS and were rebuking the UK for its official silence on the visit.

item.title: Start the week with a film: In ‘Unidentified’, lifting the veil off murder in a conservative society
item.description: Haifaa al-Mansour’s Arabic film is out on Prime Video.
item.content:encoded:
Cultural context is everything in Unidentified (2025). The film’s synopsis – a woman who is a fan of true crime shows gets obsessed with identifying a murdered Jane Doe – sounds garden variety. But the setting – Riyadh in conservative Saudi Arabia – makes all the difference.

Nawal (Mila Alzahrani) works at a police station’s archive, digitising files all day long. She’s the only woman around when her boss Majid (Shafi Al Harthi) is informed about a dead teenager lying in the desert. The girl, later named as Amal, is going to be buried in an unmarked grave.

Although it’s none of Nawal’s business, she makes it her own. Over Majid’s objections, Nawal starts investigating Amal’s background. Nawal runs into barriers every step of the way – at Amal’s school, from her circle of friends, and finally from her family.

item.title: Remembering ‘Got Japan’: This book dissects upper-caste life in Himalayan towns in colonised India
item.description: An excerpt from the Introduction to ‘Brahmins of the Himalaya: Upper-Caste Ways of Belonging, 1850-1950’, by Sanjay Joshi.
item.content:encoded:
In 1906, a young Brahmin named Bholadutt Pande decided to travel to Japan and the United States to seek better educational opportunities than were available to him in British India. He was the first from his community of elite Almora Brahmins to make a journey crossing the seas, at least in recent memory. His return to Almora in 1910 sparked a huge controversy. Overseas travel was regarded as taboo for caste-Hindus. It was impossible, some Hindus argued, to sustain the required levels of ritual purity – an essential component of caste – through a long sea voyage and an extended sojourn abroad. So Bholadutt’s return polarised the community.

Several families in Almora bore the brunt of the controversy created by Pande’s travel overseas. With such virulence did the debate on his return escalate that it created a huge schism among clans. The divisions were pretty serious – inter-family and even intra-family. Daughters could not meet mothers on account of their opposing views of the affair, fathers refused to eat with their sons, uncles ostracised nephews, brothers refused to talk to brothers – all on account of a difference of opinion on what Bholadutt Pande’s status should be. item.title: In a first, Gauhati HC asks Assam government to pay Rs 2 lakh to woman pushed into Bangladesh
item.description: Mumtaz Begum had been arrested from Nagaon foreigners tribunal in violation of the court order.
item.content:encoded:
The Gauhati High Court has directed the Assam government to pay Rs 2 lakh as compensation to a Bengali-origin Muslim woman for expelling her to Bangladesh.

This is the first time any court has imposed a cost on the state for forcing out a person to Bangladesh, in violation of deportation rules.

As Scroll had reported, Mumtaz Begum’s family realised she had been forced out of the country when they filed a habeas corpus petition in the Gauhati High Court.

The High Court impleaded the Ministry of External Affairs in the case and said it would direct it to “make an endeavour to have the woman located in Bangladesh and to expatriate her to India”.

The court also came down heavily on the Nagaon foreigners tribunal for its role in Begum’s expulsion.

Acting on the habeas corpus petition, the bench of Justice Kalyan Rai Surana and Justice Susmita Phukan Khaund said the court is satisfied from the nature of action taken by the foreigners tribunal that “the element of malice in law on part of the learned tribunal is apparent on the face of record.”

item.title: Long gaps between meals affect older people differently, shows study
item.description: Ageing changes how people digest food, absorb nutrients, control blood sugar and maintain muscle.
item.content:encoded:
Going for much of the day without eating is often promoted as a way to improve health or lose weight. But a new study suggests that long gaps between meals may have different effects on older adults – especially those in the oldest age groups.

For the study, my colleagues and I followed nearly 3,000 people aged 60 and over in Sweden and found that those who usually went longest without eating developed chronic diseases faster than those who had shorter gaps between meals. The difference was clearest among people aged 78 and over.

This does not mean that fasting causes disease in old age, nor that every older person should avoid long intervals without food. But it does raise questions about whether advice based on studies of younger and middle-aged adults can be safely applied to older age groups.

Fasting helps the body switch from using readily available sugar to using stored energy, such as fat. Studies in younger adults have linked some forms of fasting to better control of blood sugar and other potentially beneficial changes in metabolism. A recent review found that intermittent fasting led to modest weight loss and some improvements in metabolic health compared with eating without restrictions.

item.title: ‘Kin’: Tayari Jones’s new novel is a story of and by women, and of their shared passions

I found myself reading slowly through Tayari Jones’s new novel, Kin till the second half, where it opened up like a flower that had been tightly furled for too long. By the final pages, I realised the significance of its epigraph – “We are each other’s business.”

At its heart, Kin is a story of and by women.

The men in the novel play their roles well. They hurt, comfort, disappoint, leave, and stay. But it is the women who are its heart. Every time I thought I understood them, they revealed yet another hidden history, an old grief, a private resilience.

item.title: In a surprising reversal of trends, world’s mangrove forests are expanding
item.description: What’s driving this? And could it help curb climate change?
item.content:encoded:
Mangroves are perplexing plants.

They breathe through their roots, appear to stand on stilts and grow best in hot, salty seawater drawn in and out by the tide.

Historically, mangrove forests have been dismissed as inhospitable places to avoid and have been extensively cleared. But these fascinating trees are now gaining attention for how they support biodiversity, store carbon and buffer the effects of storms, cyclones and tsunamis.

Since 1984, scientists have been monitoring the growth and geographical reach of mangrove forests using satellites. And for the first time, these unique ecosystems are expanding at a faster rate than they are declining.

So what’s driving this? And could it help curb climate change?

Why mangroves matter

Mangrove forests were long viewed as largely expendable places. Research shows people were quick to convert them into rice paddies, oil palm plantations and aquaculture operations. Some were even used as rubbish tips.

However, mangrove forests are now recognised as a vital part of our coastal environments. They provide habitat for a wealth of plants and animals including fish such as barramundi and giant shovelnose rays, reptiles such as seasnakes and even mammals such as the proboscis monkey and water mouse. They are crucial carbon stores, locking up roughly four times more carbon than other land-based forests. Mangroves can also shelter coastal communities and ecosystems from natural disasters by reducing the risk of flooding and erosion.
